validators: Petrie 1883 via the Birdsall transcription; Dash 2015; HYG v4.1; ERFA 2.0.1.5 ltp

claims.title: Base side 756 ft
claims.wonder: Each side of the Great Pyramid is 756 feet long.
claims.test: 755.78 ft (230.363 m). 756 ft rounds it; the design is 440 royal cubits.

claims.title: Height 480 ft without the capstone, 1/11 mile
claims.wonder: Without its capstone it stood 480 feet: one eleventh of a mile.
claims.test: 5280/11 = 480 is true arithmetic. The surveyed apex height is about 481.3 ft (146.7 m). 480 ft 'without the capstone' needs a cap only 0.4 m tall; the pyramidion is lost and its size unknown (Amenemhat III's surviving one is about 1.3 m).

claims.title: Height : base = 7 : 11
claims.wonder: Height to base is 7 to 11, a ratio you can count on your fingers.
claims.test: 0.6368 against 0.6364: 280 : 440 royal cubits, the slope of a seked of 5 1/2 palms per cubit.

claims.title: Base area about 13 acres
claims.wonder: The base covers thirteen acres.

claims.title: 2.3 million blocks
claims.wonder: Two million three hundred thousand blocks.
claims.test: An estimate (volume about 2.6 million m3 over an assumed mean block), never a count.

claims.title: Perimeter / (2 x height) = pi
claims.wonder: Walk around the base, divide by twice the height: π.
claims.test: The reference square-pyramid model yields 2b/h ≈ 3.140160, near π. A 5½-palm seked yields 22/7 exactly. The default comparison uses analytic geometry; the inherited receipt's last digits are finite Monte Carlo sample means. Historical slope ranges are not calibrated standard deviations.
claims.originalTest: 3.1401 +/- 0.0037: pi to 3 significant digits. The seked of 5 1/2 palms makes it 22/7 = 3.1429 by design, so this pi is the builders' 22/7, not the transcendental number.
claims.reviewNote: A 5½-palm seked mathematically produces 22/7 for this ratio. That identity does not establish which constant, if any, the builders intended.

claims.title: Perimeter / height = tau (2 pi)
claims.wonder: The perimeter divided by the height is 2π: the pyramid is a squared circle.
claims.test: The same ratio as pi, doubled: 6.280. One coincidence, not two.

claims.title: Slant height / half-base = phi
claims.wonder: The sloping face divided by half the base is the golden ratio.
claims.test: 1.6195 +/- 0.0012 against 1.6180: phi to 3 significant digits. 14/11 gives 1.6186. pi and phi cannot both be meant exactly: the pi slope is 51.854 deg, the phi slope 51.827 deg, and the survey (51.867 +/- 0.033 deg) cannot tell them apart.

claims.title: Khafre's pyramid is a 3-4-5 triangle
claims.wonder: Half the base, the height and the sloping face of the second pyramid stand as 3 : 4 : 5, the first Pythagorean triple.
claims.test: Petrie's casing angle is 53°10′ ± 4′; a 3-4-5 face is 53.1301° (53°07′48″), inside his error. The height a 3-4-5 needs is 5649.9 in against his 5,664 ± 13 in (1.08 errors). In Egyptian terms this is a seked of 5¼ palms, the slope the Rhind papyrus uses in its pyramid problems. Designed, most likely, but as a builder's ratio: no evidence they knew 3²+4²=5² as a theorem.
claims.source: Petrie 1883 s.66 (base mean 8474.9 in), s.67 (53°10′ ± 4′; height 5,664 ± 13 in)

claims.title: Menkaure repeats the Great Pyramid's slope
claims.wonder: The third pyramid rises at the same 51° and a fraction as the first: the π slope, a third of the size.
claims.test: Petrie: 51°0′ ± 10′ (or 51°10′30″ from the granite courses); seked 5½ gives 51°50′34″, five of his errors away, and a 5:4 rise-to-run gives 51°20′25″, two errors away. A steep-fifties family slope, yes; the same π slope, not shown.
claims.source: Petrie 1883 s.80 (base mean 4153.6 in), s.81 (51°0′ ± 10′; height 2564 ± 15 in)
claims.originalTitle: Menkaure repeats the Great Pyramid's slope
claims.originalTest: Petrie: 51°0′ ± 10′ (or 51°10′30″ from the granite courses); seked 5½ gives 51°50′34″, five of his errors away, and a 5:4 rise-to-run gives 51°20′25″, two errors away. A steep-fifties family slope, yes; the same π slope, not shown.
claims.reviewNote: The same-slope claim is unsupported by the cited values: the difference is about 0.85°, approximately five times the quoted 10′ range. Broad family resemblance is a weaker statement than equality.

claims.title: The slope is a seked of 5½ palms
claims.wonder: Rise one cubit, run five and a half palms. One rule, repeated for every casing stone, makes the whole shape.
claims.test: Seked 5½ is 51°50′34″; Petrie measured 51°52′ ± 2′, 1.4′ away. This is the simplest account of the shape: it uses the Egyptians' own slope unit, known from the Rhind papyrus, and it brings 22/7 for π with it for free.
claims.source: Petrie 1883 s.25 (51°52′ ± 2′); Rhind Mathematical Papyrus problems 56-60 for the seked

claims.title: π and φ both live in the one slope
claims.wonder: The same triangle gives the circle's number and the golden number. Two of the deepest constants in one pile of stone.
claims.test: They are one fact. 4 ÷ √φ = 3.14461, within 0.1 % of π, for any triangle ever drawn. A π pyramid slopes at 51°51′14″ and a φ pyramid at 51°49′38″: 1.6′ apart, less than Petrie's ± 2′. No survey can tell them apart, and the seked of 5½ (51°50′34″) sits between them.

claims.title: Each face has the area of the height squared
claims.wonder: Said to come from Herodotus: the square on the height equals a face.
claims.test: Face 21,485 m² against height² 21,527 m²: 0.20 % apart. It is the φ claim again in other words (it holds exactly for a golden pyramid). The wording was put into Herodotus's mouth by John Taylor in 1859; I did not find it in the Histories in this session.
claims.source: Dash 2015 base, Petrie slope; attribution not re-read: Suspected

claims.title: Khafre's pyramid is built on the number 137
claims.wonder: Its base is 411 cubits: three times 137. Its height is 274: twice 137. And 137 is the fine-structure number that governs light and matter.
claims.test: True arithmetic: 8,474.9 in ÷ 20.620 = 411.0 cubits = 3 × 137.00, and 1/α = 137.036. Nobody claims this. This page's own search turned it up in a minute, which is the point: a 3-4-5 pyramid of 411 cubits has to contain 137, and there are many famous numbers to bump into.
claims.source: Petrie 1883 s.66, s.136; CODATA 1/α. An invented claim, made here to show how easy they are

claims.title: The royal cubit is π/6 of a metre
claims.wonder: Divide π by six and you get 0.5236. That is the royal cubit in metres, a unit defined in France in 1791.
claims.test: Petrie's cubit is 20.620 ± 0.005 in = 0.52375 ± 0.00013 m; π/6 = 0.52360 m sits 1.17 Petrie errors below it. Three literal digits agree. The metre was defined 4,300 years later from a survey of the Paris meridian, so the match cannot have been designed; and a 0.52 m cubit is simply forearm-sized.

claims.title: 440 cubits wide, 280 cubits high
claims.wonder: In the builders' own unit the pyramid is two round numbers.
claims.test: Base ÷ 440 = 20.611 in and height ÷ 280 = 20.629 in, against Petrie's independent cubit of 20.620 ± 0.005 in: the base cubit is 1.8 errors under, the height cubit is inside the height's own ± 7 in. Petrie: 'Outside form of Pyramid is 280 and 440 cubits, confirmed by the π theory.'

claims.title: The perimeter is 1,760 cubits, and a mile is 1,760 yards
claims.wonder: Walk around the pyramid: 1,760 cubits. Walk a mile: 1,760 yards.
claims.test: 4 × 440 = 1,760 exactly, by design. The mile got its 1,760 yards in England in 1593 (8 furlongs of 220 yards). Two true numbers with no link: a cubit is not a yard, and the pyramid's perimeter is 0.573 of a mile.

claims.title: The base is 365.24 sacred cubits: one for each day of the year
claims.wonder: Piazzi Smyth, Astronomer Royal for Scotland, 1864: the side of the base counts the days of the year.
claims.test: Petrie's base is 9,068.8 ± 0.5 in, which is 362.39 'sacred cubits' of 25.025 in, not 365.24: 0.8 % short. Smyth had measured over rubble. Petrie, who went to Giza to test this, wrote: 'there is no authentic example, that will bear examination, of the use or existence of any such measure as a Pyramid inch.'

claims.title: The perimeter is 36,524 inches: the days in a hundred years
claims.wonder: A calendar in stone.
claims.test: Petrie's perimeter is 36,275 in (36,239 'pyramid inches'): 0.8 % short of 36,524.

claims.title: The King's Chamber hides a 3-4-5 triangle in three dimensions
claims.wonder: The room is 10 by 20 cubits. Its height is 5√5 cubits, so the end-wall diagonal is 15, the floor is 20 long, and the diagonal through the room is 25: a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by five.
claims.test: Length ÷ width is 2.0000: the 10 × 20 cubit plan is real. The height that closes the triangle is 230.45 in; Petrie measured 230.09 ± 0.15 in from the floor, 2.4 of his errors short (0.16 %). This is Petrie's own theory (squares of 100, 400 and 125 square cubits) and he judged it to agree 'within little more than the small range of the probable errors'. One free choice remains: the walls run 5.11 in below the floor, and from the wall base the triangle fails.
claims.source: Petrie 1883 s.155 (206.12, 412.24, 230.09 ± .15 in; floor raised 5.11 ± .12 in above the wall base), s.55 and s.64 (levels)
claims.originalTitle: The King's Chamber hides a 3-4-5 triangle in three dimensions
claims.originalTest: Length ÷ width is 2.0000: the 10 × 20 cubit plan is real. The height that closes the triangle is 230.45 in; Petrie measured 230.09 ± 0.15 in from the floor, 2.4 of his errors short (0.16 %). This is Petrie's own theory (squares of 100, 400 and 125 square cubits) and he judged it to agree 'within little more than the small range of the probable errors'. One free choice remains: the walls run 5.11 in below the floor, and from the wall base the triangle fails.
claims.reviewNote: The inherited Confirmed grade applied to the separate 2:1 floor plan. The displayed height/spatial-diagonal relationship was qualified as Likely in the original calculation. Historical quoted errors are not treated here as calibrated Gaussian standard deviations.

claims.title: The King's Chamber floor sits where the pyramid is half its base
claims.wonder: Cut the pyramid level with the chamber floor: the slice is exactly half the area of the base.
claims.test: Half area comes at height × (1 − 1/√2) = 1691.8 in. Petrie levelled the floor at 1,692.8 ± 0.6 in: 1.0 in apart on a height known to ± 7 in. One of the tightest matches in the building, and it uses nothing but the pyramid's own height.
claims.source: Petrie 1883 s.25 (height), s.55 and s.64 (floor level)

claims.title: The Queen's Chamber is at half the King's Chamber's height
claims.wonder: One chamber exactly halfway up to the other.
claims.test: Queen's floor 834.4 in, half of the King's 1,692.8 is 846.4: 12.0 in out (1.4 %). The Queen's floor is rough and may have lost a paving course; with 12 in of paving it would fit.

claims.title: The Queen's Chamber ridge is on the pyramid's exact middle
claims.wonder: The roof ridge of the Queen's Chamber lies in the east-west plane through the apex.
claims.test: Petrie: 'the ridge of the roof is exactly in the mid-place of the Pyramid, equidistant from N. and S. sides'; his table puts it 0.3 ± 0.8 in north of centre. The King's Chamber, by contrast, is 11.0 m south of centre.

claims.title: The entrance passage falls 1 in 2
claims.wonder: Down into the rock for a hundred metres, one unit down for every two along.
claims.test: 1 in 2 is 26°33′54″; Petrie's mean axis is 26°31′23″ ± 5″: 2.5′ apart over 105 m, a drift of 8 cm. The Ascending Passage (26°02′30″) and Grand Gallery (26°16′40″) follow the same rule more loosely. Petrie: 'far more accurate than any other theory'.

claims.title: The coffer's outside is twice its inside
claims.wonder: The granite box in the King's Chamber: its outer volume is exactly double what it holds.
claims.test: Petrie: contents 72,030 in³, solid bulk 70,500, over all 142,530. Outside ÷ inside = 1.979, 1.1 % under 2; the granite and the hollow differ by 2.2 %. Rough-sawn granite with saw marks still on it: a round ratio aimed at, not hit.

claims.title: Base level to within 15 mm
claims.wonder: The whole base is level to the width of a thumb.
claims.test: Reported deviation of the platform is about 2.1 cm (secondary report of the Cole/Lehner work); Petrie found a 40 ft stretch of the first course level to 0.02 in. Same order of magnitude, not the exact 15 mm.

claims.title: Casing joints under 0.5 mm
claims.wonder: The casing joints are thinner than a fingernail.
claims.test: Petrie's mean joint thickness is 1/50 inch (0.51 mm), measured on the few casing stones left at the base.
claims.originalTest: Petrie's mean joint thickness is 1/50 inch (0.51 mm), measured on the few casing stones left at the base.
claims.reviewNote: A reported mean of 0.508 mm does not establish an upper bound below 0.5 mm. Individual widths and measurement uncertainty are not supplied. Tight workmanship remains impressive; the literal threshold is unestablished.

claims.title: Aligned to true north within 0.1%
claims.wonder: It faces true north more exactly than the Greenwich observatory was built.
claims.test: About 3 arcminutes west of north (0.052 deg). '0.1%' is a loose way to say it: as a fraction of a full turn the error is 0.014%.

claims.title: Four sides equal to within two inches
claims.wonder: Four sides of 230 metres that differ by less than the width of your hand.
claims.test: Petrie's casing sides: N 9,069.4, E 9,067.7, S 9,069.5, W 9,068.6 in. Spread 1.8 in (4.6 cm) in 9,069: 1 part in 5,038. Corner angles are out by a mean of 12 seconds of arc.

claims.title: The three south-east corners lie on one line
claims.wonder: A ruler laid on the south-east corners of all three pyramids touches each one, and points to Heliopolis.
claims.test: The line through Khufu's and Khafre's south-east corners passes 22.3 m from Menkaure's, over a run of 929 m: 1.4° out of line. Close enough to look planned from the ground, not a surveyed line. The Heliopolis bearing is not tested here.

claims.title: Khafre stands on the Great Pyramid's diagonal
claims.wonder: Extend the diagonal of the first pyramid to the south-west and it runs through the heart of the second.
claims.test: Khafre's centre is 334.4 m west and 353.9 m south of Khufu's: 13.8 m off the 45° diagonal, on a base 215 m wide. It passes through the pyramid, not through its centre.

claims.title: The Great Pyramid has eight sides
claims.wonder: At dawn on the equinox a shadow line splits each face in two: the faces are dished, and the pyramid has eight sides, not four.
claims.test: The core masonry is hollowed along the middle of each face; Petrie measured it and aerial photographs show it. Whether the finished casing was dished, and whether it was meant, are open. The equinox story is modern. Not measured in this session.
claims.source: Petrie 1883 (hollowing of the core faces), not re-read here

claims.title: Latitude of the Grand Gallery's centre = 29.9792458 N
claims.wonder: The latitude of the Great Pyramid is 29.9792458° N. The speed of light is 299,792,458 m/s.
claims.test: The selected 29.9792458° line crosses the illustrative footprint about 7.8 m north of the adopted map centre, roughly 12.5 m south of the modeled Gallery midpoint. The chosen point, datum, coordinate notation and modern SI units determine this numerical resemblance. It does not establish knowledge of the vacuum speed of light.
claims.originalTitle: Latitude of the Grand Gallery's centre = 29.9792458 N
claims.originalTest: A 1e-7 degree step is 1.1 cm, so the 230 m pyramid spans about 20800 such latitude lines; one of them must read 29.9792458, and it lies 7.8 m north of the centre, inside the Gallery but 12.5 m south of the Gallery's midpoint (29.979358 N). The building supports 4 to 5 significant digits (29.979). The summit disk on the old Egyptian datum reads 29.978995 N; moved to WGS84 it is 29.979161 N: the datum alone moves the 4th decimal place. The metre is from 1791 and the second's value for c was fixed in 1983.
claims.reviewNote: The target happens to fall within the modeled extent; many possible latitude lines do not logically force any selected target to lie there. The centre/datum accuracy does not justify centimetre interpretation of seven displayed decimals.

claims.title: The pyramid is the northern hemisphere at 1 : 43,200
claims.wonder: 43,200 is half the seconds in a day. Multiply the perimeter by it and you get the Earth's equator.
claims.test: Perimeter × 43,200 = 39806.7 km against 40,075.0 km: 0.67 % short. The scale that fits the equator is 1 : 43,491, a number nobody has a story for.

claims.title: … and its height is the polar radius
claims.wonder: Multiply the height by the same 43,200 and you get the distance from the Earth's centre to the pole.
claims.test: Height × 43,200 = 6338.3 km against 6,356.8 km: 0.29 % short. Both matches are one fact, not two: the pyramid's perimeter ÷ height is 2π to 3 digits (the seked), and so is equator ÷ radius. Once the scale fits one, the other is free.

claims.title: The two circles of the base differ by the speed of light
claims.wonder: Draw one circle around the base and one inside it. Subtract their lengths: 299.79 metres. Light: 299.79 million metres a second.
claims.test: π × 230.363 × (√2 − 1) = 299.77 ± 0.09 m, against 299.792: four literal digits, and the survey cannot say more. It is the base length in disguise: any square of side 230.39 m does this, and the base is 440 cubits. Metres and seconds came 4,300 years later.

claims.title: The pyramid's mass, times a thousand million million, is the Earth's
claims.wonder: 5.97 million tonnes of stone. The Earth: 5.97 million million million million kilograms.
claims.test: Volume 2.595 million m³. To give 5.972 × 10⁹ kg the mean density must be 2.30 t/m³. Limestone runs 2.2 to 2.6, and nobody knows the pyramid's mean density: bedrock core, voids, mortar, granite. The match is a choice of density.
claims.source: Dash 2015 base, Petrie slope; IAU Earth mass

claims.title: It stands one third of the way from the equator to the pole
claims.wonder: Latitude thirty: a third of the way up the world.
claims.test: The centre is at 29.9792° N: 1.25′ short of 30°, or 2.3 km. Good, and easy to do with a gnomon; the plateau's northern edge stops you going further. The usual 'correction for refraction' story is not needed.

claims.title: The pyramid stands at the centre of the Earth's land
claims.wonder: Its parallel and its meridian cross more dry land than any others on Earth.
claims.test: Not tested here: it needs a global land map and a definition of 'centre'. Published checks put the longest-land meridian and parallel elsewhere. Kept in the atlas so that 'untested' has an honest row.

claims.title: 86 400 seconds in a day
claims.wonder: A day has 86,400 seconds.
claims.test: True by definition: 24 x 60 x 60.

claims.title: Sun's diameter 864 000 miles
claims.wonder: The Sun is 864,000 miles across: the day's number, times ten.
claims.test: 864 576 miles from the IAU nominal solar radius: 864 000 is 0.07% low.

claims.title: Sun's radius 432 000 miles
claims.wonder: The Sun's radius is 432,000 miles.
claims.test: 432 288 miles: 0.07% off. Only in miles: 695 700 km.

claims.title: Moon's radius 1 080 miles
claims.wonder: The Moon's radius is 1,080 miles.
claims.test: 1 079.6 miles: 0.04% off. Only in miles: 1 737.4 km.

claims.title: The Sun is 108 Earths wide
claims.wonder: 108 Earths fit across the Sun.
claims.test: 109.2 (mean Earth radius 6 371 km): 1% off.

claims.title: The Sun is 108 of its own diameters away
claims.wonder: The Sun stands 108 of its own diameters away.
claims.test: 107.5 on the mean distance; 105.7 to 109.3 over the year.

claims.title: Meridian 40 000 km
claims.wonder: A meridian through the poles is 40,000 km.
claims.test: 40 007.86 km. True because the metre was defined from it in 1791: it says nothing about Giza.

claims.title: Moon 400 times smaller than the Sun
claims.wonder: The Moon is 400 times smaller than the Sun…

claims.title: Moon 400 times closer than the Sun
claims.wonder: …and 400 times nearer, so they look the same size.
claims.test: 389 on mean distances; it swings from about 363 to 425 over the orbits.

claims.title: Earth rotates 400 times faster than the Moon
claims.wonder: …and the Earth turns 400 times faster than the Moon.
claims.test: 27.4 times faster (sidereal days). No reading gives 400.

claims.title: The height times a billion is the distance to the Sun
claims.wonder: Stack a thousand million Great Pyramids and you reach the Sun.
claims.test: Height × 10⁹ = 146.7 million km against 149.6 million: 1.9 % short, and the Earth's own distance swings between 147.1 and 152.1 million km each year, so it lands below even the closest approach. Powers of ten are free in the metric system the builders did not have.
claims.originalTitle: The height times a billion is the distance to the Sun
claims.originalTest: Height × 10⁹ = 146.7 million km against 149.6 million: 1.9 % short, and the Earth's own distance swings between 147.1 and 152.1 million km each year, so it lands below even the closest approach. Powers of ten are free in the metric system the builders did not have.
claims.reviewNote: Approximation only: the comparison is about 1.92% short and below the stated orbital-distance range. The retained editorial grade does not certify equality or agreement within a measurement uncertainty.

claims.title: Set the Moon on the Earth and you have drawn the Great Pyramid
claims.wonder: Earth's radius for the half-base, Earth plus Moon for the height: the triangle has the pyramid's slope.
claims.test: (Earth + Moon) ÷ Earth = 1.27270; the pyramid's 14/11 is 1.27273: five literal digits. The slope it gives is 51°50′32″ against Petrie's 51°52′ ± 2′. The strangest match in the atlas, and it is about the Earth and Moon, whose sizes no builder could know: the Moon's radius is 0.2727 of the Earth's, and 3/11 is 0.2727.
claims.source: IUGG mean Earth radius 6,371.0088 km; Moon 1,737.4 km

claims.title: Earth's radius plus the Moon's is 5,040 miles: 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 × 5 × 6 × 7
claims.wonder: Plato's perfect number of citizens, written in the sky.

claims.title: Earth's diameter is 7,920 miles: 8 × 9 × 10 × 11
claims.test: Mean diameter 7917.5 miles: 0.03 % under. Only in miles.

claims.title: The three pyramids are Orion's belt laid on the ground
claims.wonder: Three stars in a slightly bent row, the third one fainter and off the line. Three pyramids in a slightly bent row, the third one smaller and off the line.
claims.test: Shape: the pyramids' spacing ratio is 1.072 against the belt's 0.979, and the bend is 11.5° against 7.2°. That is a fair likeness, 4 degrees apart in the bend. Against it: the brightest belt star is the middle one (Alnilam, 1.69 mag) while the biggest pyramid is the end one; to lay the belt on the plan you must put south at the top; and three points always make a bent row, so only two numbers (ratio and bend) are tested. Pin the two end stars on Khufu and Menkaure and the middle star lands 28 m from Khafre's centre (its base is 215 m wide); and the pinned map sits 36° away from south-up in 2560 BC, 13° in 10,500 BC. Bauval's wider map (Dahshur, Abu Roash as other Orion stars) is not tested here.
claims.source: Petrie 1883 s.92 centre offsets (13931.6, 13165.8; 15170.4, 9450.2 in; the transcription flags the derived distances of this table as needing correction); HYG v4.1 with space motion; ERFA ltp

claims.title: Four shafts aim at four stars
claims.wonder: From the King's Chamber one shaft points at Orion's belt and one at the pole star of the age. From the Queen's Chamber, one at Sirius and one at the Little Dipper. All four, in the century the pyramid was built.
claims.test: In 2560 BC the four stars crossed the meridian -0.33°, -1.14°, -0.62° and 0.62° from the shaft angles. Each shaft matches its star exactly in a different year: KS 2492 BC, KN 2357 BC, QS 2359 BC, QN 2383 BC. The spread is 135 years, and all four dates fall after Khufu's reign, so the shafts cannot date the pyramid to better than about a century (Thuban also fits a second time, in 3237 BC, on its way in to the pole); and the shafts bend on their way out, so 'the' angle is itself a choice (Petrie and Gantenbrink differ by up to 2°).
claims.source: Shaft angles: Gantenbrink 1993 as commonly cited (not re-read in this session: Likely); Petrie 1883 s.56 (31°33′, 45°13′40″), s.44 (37°28′, 38°28′). Sky: HYG v4.1 space motion + ERFA ltp; geometric altitudes, no refraction

claims.title: Thuban stood still over the pyramid
claims.wonder: When the pyramid was built the sky turned around Thuban, in the Dragon, not around Polaris.
claims.test: Thuban was 1.34° from the pole in 2560 BC and closest, 0.10°, in 2796 BC. Polaris was then 25.3° away. Today Polaris is 0.63° off.

claims.title: The two base diagonals add up to the years of the precession
claims.wonder: 25,827 pyramid inches across the diagonals: the Great Year, the slow wobble of the Earth's axis.
claims.test: With Petrie's base the diagonals sum to 25,625 pyramid inches. The precession takes about 25,772 years today, and its rate changes: 0.6 % apart, 2 digits. It needed Smyth's too-long base to work.
claims.source: Petrie 1883 s.21; IAU 2006 precession rate 50.288″ per year

claims.title: The entrance passage is a telescope aimed at the pole star
claims.wonder: Sir John Herschel, 1836: from the bottom of the passage the old pole star Thuban shone straight down it, in 2170 BC.
claims.test: Thuban at its lowest stood 26°31′23″ above the horizon in 3,409 BC and 2,185 BC: those are the dates the passage fits, and Herschel's 2170 BC is close to the second. In 2560 BC it stood at 28.64°, 2.1° too high. So the passage does not date the pyramid; the 1 in 2 slope explains the angle with no star at all.
claims.source: Petrie 1883 s.36; HYG v4.1 + ERFA ltp; Herschel's date as commonly cited

claims.title: In 10,500 BC the Sphinx watched its own image rise
claims.wonder: A lion, facing due east. On the spring equinox of 10,500 BC the constellation of the Lion rose before the Sun.
claims.test: On that date Regulus lay 21° and Denebola 2° from the equinox point along the ecliptic, both behind it: the spring Sun stood just past Leo's tail, so Leo did rise ahead of it. In 2560 BC the equinox point was 7° from Aldebaran, in the Bull. The sky fits; the date is chosen to make it fit, and the star-figure 'Leo' is not attested in Egypt that early.
claims.source: HYG v4.1 + ERFA ltp and ltpecl (ecliptic of date)

claims.title: 10,500 BC is when Orion stood lowest in the sky
claims.wonder: The belt swings up and down over 26,000 years. The pyramids mark the bottom of the swing: the First Time.
claims.test: Alnitak's lowest culmination at Giza in this model is 9.1° in 10,701 BC (highest 58.2° in AD 2400). So yes, the low point falls near 10,500 BC. The link to the pyramids is the belt-map rotation, which fits 23° better then than in 2560 BC but still misses by 13°.
claims.source: HYG v4.1 + ERFA ltp (Vondrak 2011, valid over this span)

claims.title: Two stars and a plumb line set the pyramid to north
claims.wonder: Kate Spence, 2000: hang a plumb line, wait until Kochab stands exactly over Mizar, and the line is north. It was true only around 2467 BC.
claims.test: In this model Kochab and Mizar stood on one vertical line through the pole in 2,465 BC; Spence gave 2467 BC from other star data. The method explains why pyramids before and after Khufu's are aligned worse, in the order the drift predicts. A way to date the pyramid by its own error; the 3′43″ error itself is Petrie's.
claims.source: HYG v4.1 + ERFA ltp; Spence 2000 (Nature) as commonly cited, not re-read here

claims.title: Greaves surveyed it in 1637
claims.wonder: John Greaves measured it with instruments in 1637.
claims.test: He was at Giza in 1638-39 and published Pyramidographia in 1646; Newton used his figures for the sacred cubit.

claims.title: Greaves inscribed one English foot in the King's Chamber
claims.wonder: He cut one English foot into the King's Chamber wall for those who would come after.
claims.test: No source found for an inscription; his book prints an English foot so that readers could compare it.

review.design_labels: Retained editorial plausibility labels; not probabilities or documentary proof of a particular ancient intention.
